articles.title: How to Test an AI Agent: Start With Error Analysis, Not Metrics
articles.excerpt: Your agent passed the demo. Does it still work on the 500th request? Agents fail differently from normal software. A normal bug throws an exception. An agent bug returns a confident, well-formatted, w…
articles.body: Your agent passed the demo. Does it still work on the 500th request? Agents fail differently from normal software. A normal bug throws an exception. An agent bug returns a confident, well-formatted, wrong answer with HTTP 200: the right tool with the wrong ID, an extra loop, a step quietly skipped. Nothing alerts you, and the only witness is an unhappy user. The good news is that you already know the fix. It's the testing discipline you practise every day, adapted to a component that is non-deterministic and takes many steps. Traces replace stack traces, eval datasets replace test fixtures, and graders replace assertions. Why agents are hard to test Four properties make agents different: Non-determinism. The same task can produce different tool sequences on different runs.

articles.title: Insurance Claims Intake Retrieval Architecture: Freshness Contracts Under Latency Budgets
articles.excerpt: Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context you can trace back to the claim record. Put a hard latency budget around each stage, and treat chunk f…
articles.body: Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context you can trace back to the claim record. Put a hard latency budget around each stage, and treat chunk freshness as a contract rather than a vague promise. An insurance claims intake flow has a nasty shape. A new claim arrives, the adjuster wants likely duplicates, and the answer has to be useful before the next screen renders. The corpus also changes while you search: a corrected loss description, a withdrawn policy note, or a deleted fraud case can make yesterday's nearest neighbor actively misleading. I build tools for developers, so I start with the stopwatch and the payload. Fancy ranking is secondary if the first call needs a pile of glue code.

Symptom urllib.request.urlopen(url) in Python returns: HTTP Error 403: Forbidden error code: 1010 The same URL opens fine in a browser and with curl . Error 1010 is Cloudflare's Browser Integrity Check rejecting the request on its signature. I checked that claim with the same Python and the same TLS stack, changing only the User-Agent header.

articles.title: Healthtech Avatar Handoffs in Node.js — Presigned S3-Compatible Storage
articles.excerpt: Use a short-lived presigned URL for each tenant's avatar, then validate the object before saving its key in your database. That keeps image bytes off the application server and makes the important dec…
articles.body: Use a short-lived presigned URL for each tenant's avatar, then validate the object before saving its key in your database. That keeps image bytes off the application server and makes the important decision explicit: an avatar is replaceable data with a deletion deadline, not a public asset or an immutable record. The useful mental model is small: Before: browser → Node.js → object storage → database. After: browser → object storage, while Node.js issues permission and records the result. The server still owns authorization. The browser receives one narrowly scoped upload URL, with an expiry and a content-type constraint. It never receives the storage service key. How should Node.js upload a user avatar to S3-compatible storage?

articles.body: Most people point Claude Code at a codebase. I pointed it at my notes. Here is the whole trick, in a form you can copy in ten minutes. 1. A CLAUDE.md with house rules Claude Code reads a CLAUDE.md in the folder it runs in. Mine says, in plain language: the folder structure (PARA: Projects, Areas, Resources, Archive, plus Inbox and Journal) the frontmatter every note needs ( type , status , created ) "never delete a note, move it to the archive" "check today's date with date , never guess" "before touching more than 10 files, show a list and ask" That last line matters more than it looks. An agent on your personal notes needs a brake. 2. Four skills instead of forty prompts A skill is just a SKILL.md in .claude/skills/<name>/ with a description (trigger phrases) and numbered steps.

articles.title: You can see another galaxy with the naked eye — here's how to find it
articles.excerpt: The Andromeda galaxy is one of the most distant things you can see with the naked eye. The difficult part isn't finding it. It's believing that faint smudge really is another galaxy.
articles.body: The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned. I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way . Would she like to see it? She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied. There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened.

articles.body: Sometimes science can seem really counter-intuitive. For example, occasionally in astronomy, you can see more with less light. Case in point: the emergence of a giant planet in observations made by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), when astronomers found a way to block out light from the planet's parent star. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , in question is 51 Eridani b (51 ERI b), a gas giant with the same mass as around 11 Jupiters that orbits a star located around 97 light-years away. 51 ERI b was discovered back in 2015 by ground-based telescopes, but the planet was missing from observations of the system made by the JWST.

articles.body: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini This NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image released Nov. 5, 2026, provides a lesson in galactic history. The sparkling collection of stars is named Messier 30 (M30) after the French astronomer, Charles Messier , who cataloged M30 and other diffuse objects that might be mistaken for comets in the early telescopes of Messier’s time. M30 lies about 27,500 light-years away in the constellation Capricornus. Read more about this group of stars and what scientists can learn from it. Image credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. articles.title: Hera probe gets 1st good look at asteroid system clobbered by NASA's DART mission | Space photo of the day for Nov. 6, 2026
articles.excerpt: The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has gotten its first close-up look at the Didymos binary asteroid, the first space rock system "punched" by humanity.
articles.body: The Didymos binary asteroid system, as seen by Europe's Hera probe. The main asteroid, Didymos, dominates the frame while just a sliver of its "moonlet," Dimorphos, is visible beneath it. ESA released this image on Nov. 5, 2026. (Image credit: ESA) The European Space Agency 's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has gotten its first close-up look at the Didymos binary asteroid system. If that system sounds familiar, it's because it made headlines in September 2022 when NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) spacecraft smashed into it. The aim of the DART mission was to test whether an impact could divert an asteroid away from a collision course with Earth. The purpose of Hera is to follow up on DART by making up-close observations of the Didymos system.
